Babesiosis Babesiosis (piroplasmosis) is an infection caused by in- traerythrocytic protozoa of the Babesia genus, which are transmitted to man by the bite of infected Ixodes ticks. Transmission by blood transfusion has also been reported. Ixodes scapularis, one of the ticks that may cause babesi- osis, may also be infected with, and transmit, Anaplasma phagocytophilum and/or Borrelia burgdorferi and there- fore the bite from this tick may lead to babesiosis, human granulocytic anaplasmosis (see Ehrlichiosis, p.168), or Lyme disease (p.177) as a single infection or as a co-infec- tion.1 Babesiosis occurs worldwide in animals. In the US, human infection is most commonly due to B. microti; the disease is much rarer in Europe where it is usually caused by B. divergens or B. bovis.1-3 Infection with the newly recognised babesia-like piroplasms WA-1 and MO-1 has also been reported in the USA.1,2 Clinical features of babesiosis acquired in the USA differ from that acquired in Europe. Infection in the USA is often asymptomatic and self-limiting, but may produce pro- longed severe viral-like illness with fever and haemolytic anaemia, particularly in patients who are asplenic, elderly, debilitated, or immunocompromised (including those in- fected with HIV). Symptoms include chills, sweating, my- algia, arthralgia, weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and headache. The most common complications are heart failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and renal failure.1-3 Co-infection with B. microti and Borrelia burg- dorferi has resulted in more severe symptoms. In Europe, infections have mostly been described in asplenic persons, in many of whom the infection was rapidly fatal. Clinical features include severe haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, pul- monary oedema, and renal failure. There is no established specific treatment for babesiosis. Treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic patients although all symptomatic patients should be treated with antibacterials to prevent the development of complica- tions.1 For serious infections, supportive therapies include red blood cell exchange transfusions to reduce parasitae- mia.
